vocabulary.definition: a situation in which countries share a similar ideology and foreign policy
giving into the demands of another
a diplomatic approach that involves escalating a conflict in the hope that the other side will back down first
non-violent protest which takes the form of a refusal to obey a law on the basis that the law is unjust
a change or alteration in long-term global weather patterns
a conflict, without an actual war, characterized by tension and competition between the principle adversaries
a preoccupation with the purchasing and accumulation of material goods
a policy or collection of polices aimed at stopping the spread of a particular ideology
to desert a nation or cause in favour of a rival nation
a period of lessening of tensions
a defence strategy that consists of having sufficient military resources to make an attack by an aggressor likely to result in the aggressor’s destruction

Dissent means disagreement expressed through speech, protest, criticism, or opposition. In liberal democracy, dissent is not simply a problem; it is a way citizens hold power accountable and expose weaknesses in policy or institutions.
The French policy of maintaining a nuclear arsenal for national defence
compulsory military service; conscription

Economic freedom includes private property, competition, entrepreneurship, and market choice. It is central to liberalism, but it can conflict with equality, environmental responsibility, or the wellbeing of vulnerable citizens.
a body of electors chosen by the voters in each state to elect the president and vice president of the U.S. (a plurality or first-past-the-post electoral system).
granting people the rights of citizens, especially the right to vote
a change in the natural world
a perspective that holds that one's own culture is superior
an ideal emphasizing the values and perspective of European tradition and institutions, often to the detriment of other people’s values
the deliberate killing of a person with the intent of ending his or her suffering
a policy of spreading ideological and political influence beyond the status quo
a revolutionary organization which promoted violence to supported the creation of an independent Quebec
an increase in the average temperature of Earth’s atmosphere
releases of carbon-dioxide, methane, and other gases that tend to trap the Sun’s heat in Earth’s atmosphere
a war that involves actual combat between military forces; the opposite of a cold war
a doctrine that promotes improvement to the standard of living or quality of life of others, often through outside intervention
pertaining to aspects of liberal democracy which suppress citizens’ civil liberties.
an act of Canadian Parliament passed in 1867, which dealt with the rights of First Nations people who signed treaties or became registered citizens under the act
a violent uprising, rebellion, or revolution directed at a government or a similar authority
the confinement of a group of people for political or military reasons
the physical and ideological divide between the liberal democracies of the West and the nations under the domination of the Soviet Union
protocol: a legally binding international plan to reduce greenhouse gas emissions
a legally binding international plan to reduce greenhouse gas emissions

Liberal democracy combines majority rule with rights, freedoms, equality, rule of law, and limits on government power. It is difficult because governments must respond to public demands while also protecting minorities and individual freedoms.
the term given to the movement to root out and expose potential communists within American society during the mid-1950s
an outbreak of disease which has spread to multiple nations in multiple regions of the world
a set of assumptions, concepts, or values which shape the way an individual view the world
or first-past-the-post, in which a candidate wins a seat based on the most votes when 3 or more candidates are running.
a practice in which an individual has more than one spouse
the percentage of the total votes cast received by a candidate or a political party
an electoral system in which candidates of a political party are elected on the basis of the share of the popular vote each political party receives in an election

Reasonable limits are restrictions on rights that can be justified in a free and democratic society. They matter because liberal societies sometimes need to balance freedom with safety, equality, order, or protection of others.
a school system created under the Indian Act which attempted to assimilate Aboriginal people
a previously independent nation that has fallen under the control or ideological influence of a larger, more powerful state

Security tests liberalism because fear can lead citizens and governments to accept limits on rights, surveillance, detention, discrimination, or stronger state power. These measures may be defended as necessary but can threaten liberty and equality.
consideration of one’s personal position, often without regard for the welfare of others
the group of nations that are subject or receptive to the domination, guidance, or influence of a superpower
a meeting between two or more heads of state
a nation with sufficient economic and military resources to have significant global influence
the use of violent means to achieve political goals
a government run by religious leaders and guided by religious doctrine

Viability means whether something can work in practice, not just whether it sounds good in theory. Related Issue 3 asks whether liberal principles can remain workable when governments face pressure from war, terrorism, poverty, inequality, economic crisis, environmental limits, or democratic weakness.
an act of law created by the Canadian government in 1914 to allow rule by decree without the consent of Parliament
a term used to describe actions taken to combat global terrorism in the wake of the 9/11 attacks on the United States
an official government document released in 1969, which attempted to further assimilate First Nations, Metis, and Inuit peoples of Canada
